evidence.quote: Building agentic pipelines that achieve high task performance while keeping cost and latency low requires jointly optimizing heterogeneous and coupled design choices, including prompts, topology, model selection, and tool policies. Manually searching this combinatorial design space is expensive and time-consuming, while existing automated optimizers typically operate within a predefined subset of this space, modify the pipeline monolithically, or provide little structured evidence for pipeline changes. To mitigate these challenges, we introduce the Decomposed Credit-Assignment Framework (DeCAF), which adapts the design space to the given benchmark and pipeline, optimizes each dimension separately, and generates reasoning traces for every decision. Given a task specification, benchmark examples, and a seed pipeline, DeCAF identifies relevant optimization dimensions and generates diverse experimental hypotheses for each. Independent coding-agent sessions then optimize each dimension under a restricted edit scope, jointly evaluating performance, inference cost, and latency while recording all hypotheses, edits, and outcomes of each experiment. A final synthesis session combines compatible findings across all dimensions and uses a component-level trajectory evaluator, which derives role-specific rubrics from each agent's instructions, to localize underperforming components and guide cross-dimension revisions. Across a diverse suite of agentic benchmarks, DeCAF improves average task performance by 2.58 percentage points, while reducing inference cost by 4.30% and end-to-end latency by 42.45% compared to the best overall baseline.

Let P 0 = ( G , Θ ) P_{0}=(G,\Theta) denote a seed agentic pipeline, where G = ( V , E ) G=(V,E) is its computational graph and Θ \Theta contains configurable choices such as prompts, model assignments, inference parameters, context policies, tools, and control flow. Executing a pipeline P P on input x x produces an output y ^ \hat{y} and a trajectory τ \tau containing intermediate node inputs, outputs, tool calls, and system state. For a development set 𝒟 dev = { x i } i = 1 N \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{dev}}=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} , we associate each pipeline with the objective vector

where q q , c c , and ℓ \ell measure task performance, inference cost, and end-to-end latency, respectively. A candidate dominates another if it achieves no lower task performance, no greater cost or latency, and strictly improves at least one objective. While objectives can be folded into a single scalar by weighted combination, e.g., 0.8 × q ⁡ ( P , x i ) − 0.1 × c ⁡ ( P , x i ) − 0.1 × ℓ ⁡ ( P , x i ) 0.8\times q(P,x_{i})-0.1\times c(P,x_{i})-0.1\times\ell(P,x_{i}) , this scalarization commits to weights before the attainable trade-offs are known, yields one operating point per run, and has well-known failure modes (e.g., non-convex regions of the frontier are unreachable by any linear weighting) ( Deb et al., 2002 ) . Therefore, rather than collapsing these objectives into a fixed weighted scalar, DeCAF maintains non-dominated candidates, preserving operating points with different deployment trade-offs. The held-out test set is not exposed during any part of DeCAF .

For every dimension D k D_{k} , DeCAF creates a copy of the seed pipeline and launches a fresh coding-agent session for optimization. The session receives the task specification, development data, dimension definition, and hypotheses ℋ k \mathcal{H}_{k} . It has a primary editable scope ℳ k \mathcal{M}_{k} and is instructed to focus its search on dimension D k D_{k} . However, supporting changes are allowed. For example, when modifying topology, new prompts need to be written for the agents. The ‘topology’ still remains the primary optimization dimension, while ‘prompt’ becomes the secondary or supportive dimension. The coding agent iteratively selects or adapts a hypothesis, implements the corresponding changes, and evaluates the candidate. Each dimension maintains a non-dominated archive

where ND \operatorname{ND} removes candidates dominated by another member of the archive. A candidate need not strictly dominate the seed to be retained. For example, a performance gain at a modest cost increase may represent a useful operating point on the observed frontier. Every attempted experiment is also recorded in a FINDINGS.md artifact. The record includes the motivating hypothesis, affected components, implemented change, measured objectives, whether the candidate was retained, observed regressions, and conclusions for later optimization. Failed experiments are preserved so that the final optimizer can avoid repeating ineffective changes and can reason about benchmark-specific trade-offs. Because all dimension-level sessions begin from the same seed and vary only their assigned design dimension, their outcomes provide controlled, conditional evidence about which classes of interventions are effective around P 0 P_{0} . To reduce the wall-clock optimization time, the sessions run in parallel. Each dimension returns its archive and findings, ( 𝒜 k , ℱ k ) (\mathcal{A}_{k},\mathcal{F}_{k}) , to the final stage.

The synthesis agent uses these diagnostics together with the successful and unsuccessful findings from the dimension-level searches. It tests combinations of promising changes and re-evaluates every composed pipeline end-to-end on D dev D_{\mathrm{dev}} . When a combination regresses, node_eval can help identify where the interaction failed and guide a targeted repair, such as changing a prompt or adjusting the information passed between stages. Importantly, node_eval is only a diagnostic tool: pipeline changes are still accepted or rejected using the task-performance, cost, and latency objectives. The synthesis stage maintains a final non-dominated archive using the same update rule as Eq. 2 . A final pipeline and harness is selected via the optimizer LLM from this archive using development-set evidence and is then evaluated on the held-out test set.

Seed pipelines and Models. Each optimization begins from a fixed seed pipeline. For AppWorld, we use a single ReAct coding harness, backed by Claude-Sonnet-4.6 at medium effort, with other Claude models as choices for optimization. For LiveCodeBench, we use a sequential generator–critic–refiner pipeline in which all three nodes are initialized with GPT-5.4-nano, and GPT-5.4 family of models given for optimization. For AgentDojo, we use the seed harness with a single-stage ReAct agent using Qwen-3.5-397b-a17b-FP8 model, and Gemma ( Team et al., 2026 ) and Qwen ( Team, 2026 ) family of models are available as optimization choices. For PostTrainBench, a single Claude Code post-training agent backed by Claude-Sonnet-5 at high effort is used as the seed. Opus and Haiku variants are given as choices for optimization. DeCAF uses Claude Code as the coding agent and uses /goal mechanism 1 1 1 https://code.claude.com/docs/en/goal to maintain the optimization objective. Every optimizer is run twice and the final table reports the average and standard error across both runs.

Table 1 reports the one-time cost and wall-clock time required to run each optimizer. Since DeCAF decomposes the search space into independent dimensions, coding agents for each dimension can run in parallel. This reduces the wall-clock time of DeCAF significantly compared to Meta-Harness, where experiments run sequentially. The only exception being PostTrainBench, where we ran each dimension sequentially due to the bottleneck on the GPU resources. This makes DeCAF 27.6 % 27.6\% faster on average ( 37.65 % 37.65\% faster if we remove PostTrainBench). However, this decomposition and better exploration comes at a cost, it increases the total cost of optimization. On average, DeCAF is 17.98 % 17.98\% more expensive than Meta-Harness. There are two major contributions of this increased cost. First, the optimizer is forced to explore performance using the stronger (and generally more expensive) models. This increases the cost of evaluation of the pipeline on the validation set. Second, the node_eval tool makes up roughly 6 % 6\% of the optimization cost of DeCAF . This tool takes in multiple trajectories of the agent which increases the input token cost. Due to the heavy cost of this tool, it is only given to the final synthesizer coding agent, not the dimension-level coding agents.

summary_override.summary_en: DeCAF divides Harness search into dimensions such as prompts, topology, model assignment, context and tool policies. It iterates using development-set execution results, retains non-dominated candidates, then uses component diagnostics to compose, repair and select a final pipeline for held-out evaluation. Diagnostics locate likely failures; admission still depends on task performance, inference cost and latency. Optimizer repeats are few, inference cost rises on some benchmarks and total optimization cost is higher, so a strictly cost-matched advantage is not established.
summary_override.summary_zh: DeCAF 将 Harness 搜索拆为提示、拓扑、模型分配、上下文和工具策略等维度，以开发集执行结果迭代修改并保留非支配候选，再用组件诊断合成、修复并选择最终程序，在留出集评测。组件诊断只定位可能的失败，准入仍依据任务表现、推理费用和延迟。优化器重复次数少，部分基准推理费用上升，优化总费用也更高，未证明严格同费用预算优势。

correction_of.summary_en: PLVR searches external tool-control programs, executes candidates and selects retained versions using teacher-action distance and training-task outcomes before freezing them for new tasks. The programs rely on a manually constructed primitive and rule library, rather than discovery from scratch.
correction_of.summary_zh: PLVR 搜索外部工具调用控制程序，实际执行候选后依据教师动作距离和训练任务结果选择保留版本，冻结后用于新任务。程序依赖人工建立的原语和规则库，不是从零自动发现。

evidence.quote: The gain is not attributed to the traces alone. The hand-written seed, Claude 5 Opus (which writes the primitives), and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (which mines the rules) all contribute, and neither frontier model is a blank slate about customer service or tool use; the ablation that removes the traces and the primitives still reaches 75.9% on Telecom (§ 5.6 ), and that ablation covers Retail and Telecom only. Inference under the program costs 5 to 10 times a vanilla run in FLOPs. All cells but the program’s Telecom cells are single runs, so differences of a few points are not resolved. The synthetic training tasks share the τ 2 \tau^{2} Retail and Telecom domains with the test suites and the LiveMCPBench format with LiveMCPBench, so domain knowledge can pass from the training set into the primitives, the rules, and the fine-tunes. The training tasks and their answers are different from the test tasks; the authors verified this.

We compiled a teacher’s procedure into a program rather than into a student’s weights: primitives authored by a frontier model from clusters of the teacher’s traces, each run by a small frozen model and verified as it runs, assembled by A ∗ over a rule library mined from the same traces under a reference-action objective, and used at inference to write the student’s chain of thought or to check the actions the student proposes. Run in front of three Nemotron base models and on its own, the one program estimates how much of each domain is procedure. On τ 2 \tau^{2} Telecom the estimate is that nearly all of it is: Granite-4.2-8B as the student goes from 43.0% to 91.2%, every Nemotron student reaches 93.3–94.4%, and no other arm passes 58.2%. On τ 2 \tau^{2} Retail the 8B student under the program is within 2.7 points of the Nemotron students; on LiveMCPBench the Nemotron students are 3 to 13 points ahead of it. On those two suites the program is competitive with the best baseline. No weights are updated, the program is the same for every base model, and the spread between base models shrinks where the program does the work. The program was produced once, at 3.0 × 10 19 3.0\times 10^{19} FLOPs, and costs 5 to 10 times a vanilla run to execute. Its output is a program rather than a checkpoint: it can be read at every step, it is the same for every base model, and it can be revised one primitive at a time.

summary_override.summary_en: PLVR searches external tool-control programs, executes candidates and selects retained versions using teacher-action distance and training-task outcomes before freezing them for new tasks. It uses a handwritten seed and a library of primitives and rules generated by frontier models from teacher traces.
